1.pericope_label: Be ye therefore followers of God, as dear children; and walk in love, as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savour

schools.summary: Read the phrase as unique and striking, fixing the imitation on love above every other attribute, and note that the command to be perfect is glossed elsewhere as being merciful; then distinguish the two nouns for Christ's death precisely, the offering being the perfect obedience of his humility and the sacrifice its completion in blood — an incidental but complete summary of the atonement.

Enter the limitation before the command runs too far: God is not to be imitated in his works of infinite power, which is impossible, but in righteousness and mercy; and take the chapter division as unhappy, since it has cut apart parts of a subject closely joined.

Press the force of the word, which properly means personating another, assuming his gait and speech — the root of our word mimic — and prefer imitation of God to imitation of Homer, Virgil or Alexander; identify the two offerings with the Hebrew meal-offering and sin-offering.

Take the imitation as putting great honour on practical religion, and read "as dear children" as its own argument, since children resemble their parents in the features of the face and the dispositions of the mind.

debates.question: How far may God be imitated?

sides.position: Not in his works of infinite power, which is impossible, but in righteousness and mercy
Chiefly in love, since the command to be perfect is glossed elsewhere as being merciful

outliers.note: Alone measures the command against classical models, asking how much more honourable it is to imitate God than Homer, Virgil or Alexander.
Alone enters the negative that the offering was made to God and not to the devil, invoking Anselm.

3.pericope_label: But fornication, and all uncleanness, or covetousness, let it not be once named among you, as becometh saints; neither filthiness, nor foolish talking, nor jesting, which are not convenient: but rather giving of thanks

schools.summary: Turn the company the word keeps into an indictment of a later age, asking why covetousness is not now ranked with the vices Paul ranks it with; distinguish two kinds of foul speech, the brutal talk of the fool and the refined versatility that fears nothing but dulness; and refuse to condemn courtesy, cheerfulness or good-natured humour along with levity.

Take the third vice in its plain sense of an immoderate desire of gain, while noting that its position may point rather to an insatiable appetite after the lusts just named; and condemn pleasantry not as mirth but as the garb under which idle talk conceals itself.

Treat the three terms as species of one thing, since the pleasure-taker never has enough any more than the miser; define the word for jesting as artfully turned discourse whose chaste words carry an obscene sense; and ask how a man who has been trifling in company can go apart to magnify God for the tongue he abused.
Report both readings of covetousness and call the love of the world spiritual idolatry, since the epicure makes a god of his belly and the covetous man of his money.

debates.question: Does the third vice named mean avarice or lust?

sides.position: Avarice, an immoderate desire of gain
An insatiable appetite after the lusts just named, from the company it keeps
Possibly both, the three terms being species of one thing
The ambiguity is instructive, since the Tenth Commandment joins the two kinds of coveting

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse into a sustained indictment of his own age for not ranking covetousness with the vices Paul ranks it with, and predicts that when it is so ranked the conversion of the world will not be far off.

5.pericope_label: For this ye know, that no whoremonger, nor unclean person, nor covetous man, who is an idolater, hath any inheritance in the kingdom of Christ and of God. Let no man deceive you with vain words: be not ye therefore partakers with them

schools.summary: Trace the descent into idolatry in two stages, resting on a gift of God until he is lost in it, then setting up another object on the vacant throne; identify the deceivers as early Antinomian Gnostics who held that what is done in the body cannot touch the soul; and decline to press the single article as proof of Christ's deity here, while granting Paul taught it elsewhere.

Answer the charge of harshness by distinguishing sentence on the sins from sentence on the sinner, since those who repent are no longer the persons they were; keep the charge of idolatry exact by noting it is not the idolatry Scripture usually condemns; and quote the excuses themselves — that this is a trivial fault, that God is not so cruel under grace.

Document the local morals from Athenaeus and Demosthenes — the temples to Venus, the division of women into three classes — and ask whether the vain words are not the teaching of the lawgivers and philosophers who upheld that system.
Name the abatement in advance: men have always said that the covetous man being an idolater is hyperbole, and by such abatements they explain away all the commandments.

debates.question: Who are the deceivers with vain words?

sides.position: An early Antinomian Gnosticism holding that what is done in the body cannot touch the soul
The lawgivers and philosophers of Greece, who upheld the local sexual system by authority and example
Friends still moving in those circles, and philosophers who defended such practices

outliers.note: Alone documents Ephesian morals from Athenaeus and Demosthenes, including the temples dedicated to Venus and the sentence dividing women into three classes.
Alone anticipates the objection rather than answering it, naming in advance the men who will call the charge of idolatry hyperbolical.

8.pericope_label: For ye were sometimes darkness, but now are ye light in the Lord: walk as children of light; for the fruit of the Spirit is in all goodness and righteousness and truth; proving what is acceptable unto the Lord

schools.summary: Make the difference between walking in darkness and being darkness the point, so that the reprobate becomes a new source of the darkness he spreads; press the metaphor of fruit literally, since light is the condition of the life that bears and darkness destroys it; and define proving as trying each case by the full light of God.

Take darkness for the whole nature of man before regeneration, since out of Christ everything lies under the prince of darkness; and insist that the trial be made by Scripture and not by human reason, which is corrupt and fallible.

Report the manuscript evidence for reading the fruit of the light rather than of the Spirit, on the ground that the Spirit is nowhere named in the context, and order the three qualities as a sequence — goodness in the disposition, righteousness in the conduct, truth directing both.

debates.question: Is the true reading "the fruit of the Spirit" or "the fruit of the light"?

sides.position: Of the light — the reading of the leading uncials and versions, and the Spirit is nowhere named in the context
Of the light, though the sense is unaffected either way

outliers.note: Alone argues that the metaphor of fruit is literally exact, since light is the physical condition of the vegetative life that bears and darkness destroys it.

11.pericope_label: And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them. For it is a shame even to speak of those things which are done of them in secret. But all things that are reproved are made manifest by the light

schools.summary: Define fellowship as keeping terms with evil rather than sharing in it, since sin prevails more by cowardly indulgence than by love of it; hold that sin may be branded without polluting the tongue by describing it; and allow that a man must sometimes turn on the light even when doing so is disgraceful.

Note that Paul forbids fellowship with the works and not with the workers, so that civil dealing is not prohibited; supply the works rather than the doers as the object of reproving; and observe that where an offence is manifest all are eager to clear themselves of guilt while few guard against connivance.

Read the works of darkness as the night mysteries celebrated in caves and kept secret on pain of death, and name the Bacchanalian rites the Roman senate itself banished; keep the personal object of the verb and let it carry testimony, conviction and rebuke together.
Apply the clause to heretical teachers, warning catechumens not even to greet a man who holds that Christ was assembled out of contributions from twenty-nine aeons.

sides.position: The works of darkness, so that reproving means bringing them to the light
The doers, so that it means testimony, conviction and rebuke of persons

debates.question: May the sins in question be described in order to condemn them?

sides.position: No — naming them raises polluting images, and pictures defile even when they condemn
Sometimes one must speak out and turn on the light, disgraceful though it is

outliers.note: Alone turns the verse against the reforming zeal of his own day, questioning whether ministers should portray such vices from the pulpit or reformers describe them to the world.
Applies the clause to Valentinian teachers, warning catechumens not even to greet them — a use that independently supports the Gnostic reading of the “vain words” earlier in the chapter.

14.pericope_label: Wherefore he saith, Awake thou that sleepest, and arise from the dead, and Christ shall give thee light

schools.summary: Dispose of both scriptural candidates for the quotation on grounds of wording and design, list the conjectures of a lost source, and conclude that the words are not Scripture though their form shows them well known — most likely an early Christian hymn, whose rhythm is rough but distinct.

Decline the search altogether and take Christ to be speaking through his ministers, since the daily object of preaching is to raise the dead; and guard the last clause against the notion that Christ's light follows our rising, when in fact his enlightening is our rising.

Print the supposed hymn in its three Greek lines while also offering the alternative that the verb is impersonal and refers to the gospel just named, so that this is the standing voice of the gospel everywhere; and press both figures, the sleeper who may be woken and the dead who can do nothing.

debates.question: Where does the quotation come from?

sides.position: From an early Christian hymn, whose rhythm survives in the Greek
From no citation at all: the verb is impersonal and refers to the gospel, or to Christ speaking through his ministers
From a lost book — a prophecy of Elijah, a writing of Jeremiah, or an apocryphal work
From no scriptural passage that can be adduced, though the form shows it well known

outliers.note: Alone prints the conjectured hymn in its three Greek lines, while also offering the quite different solution that the verb is impersonal and the speaker is the gospel itself.

15.pericope_label: See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil. Wherefore be ye not unwise, but understanding what the will of the Lord is

schools.summary: Correct "circumspectly" to strictly or accurately, so that the idea is finding the clear line of right and keeping to it rather than looking about for dangers; render the next phrase as the opportunity rather than the time, and draw the lesson of the unjust steward, that the children of light should show the shrewdness of the world's buyers and sellers.

Set the believer in a crowded theatre, living under the eye of God and of angels; and price the redemption of opportunity as withdrawal from the allurements that lead men astray and the abandoning of every hindrance.

Trace the word for wisdom through Pythagoras's coinage of philosopher and give the empty Gentile philosopher the name of fool; and read the walking exactly as getting to the highest pitch of every point of holiness, buying every moment out of the hands of sloth and ease.
Supply the persecuted setting — cities at war with them, households divided — and read the command as meaning that they should give no handle for hatred on any score except the gospel itself.

Make time a talent given by God and misspent whenever it is not employed to his design, and turn the common complaint round — people apt to complain of bad times would do better to let that stir them to redeem the time.

sides.position: No — it means strictly or accurately, of finding the line of right and keeping to it
The traditional sense will serve: watchful care against surrounding temptations

outliers.note: Alone supplies the persecuted setting — cities at war with the Christians and households divided — and reads the command as forbidding any handle for hatred except the gospel itself.
Alone turns the complaint about bad times into an argument for redeeming the time.

18.pericope_label: And be not drunk with wine, wherein is excess; but be filled with the Spirit; speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord

schools.summary: Analyse drunkenness not as an appetite gratified but as a reckless pursuit of excitement, confused in the Dionysiac frenzy with divine inspiration; separate the three kinds of song by their music rather than their authorship, and cite Pliny's description of Christians singing among themselves by turns.

Derive the word for excess from a negative and the verb to save, so that it pictures a man past saving, and note that where wine reigns profligacy follows of course; set the boundaries of the prohibition carefully, since it is a habit and not a single act that makes a drunkard.

Read the whole against the Bacchic rites, where priests professed to be filled with the god they served and delivered oracles in that condition; distinguish psalms, extemporary hymns and premeditated odes, and infer from the absence of inspired Christian songs that the larger effusion of the Spirit was meant to supply the lack.
Quote the clause among a catena of texts proving that the Holy Spirit subsists, lives and speaks.

debates.question: What are the psalms, hymns and spiritual songs?

sides.position: Three names for the one Book of Psalms
Distinct kinds: the psalter, extemporary hymns under the Spirit, and premeditated odes
Distinguished by their music: accompanied psalter, purely vocal hymns of the church's own making
New Christian composition is implied, the Spirit's larger effusion supplying what was not given in writing

outliers.note: Alone infers from the absence of inspired songs for the Christian dispensation that the larger effusion of the Spirit was meant to supply the lack.
His block here is the same catechetical section that the source also files at the next verse and at another chapter entirely: it quotes the verse rather than expounding it.

20.pericope_label: Giving thanks always for all things unto God and the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ; submitting yourselves one to another in the fear of God

schools.summary: Report the reading that makes the thanksgiving be offered for all persons rather than all things; describe unbroken thankfulness as the inner music of Christian life and the invariable element of public worship; and suspect that the New Testament's frequent insistence on subjection answers a real tendency to disregard restraint in the first exuberance of liberty.

Refuse to exempt anyone from mutual subjection, not even kings and governors, whose authority exists for the community's service; and point to the fear named in the clause as the only thing that can subdue our fierceness — while suspecting that the variant reading was introduced by someone who found the received phrase harsh.

Ground thanksgiving in the doctrine that all things work together for good; report the manuscript evidence for the fear of Christ rather than of God while holding that neither reading changes the sense; and warn against tenacity over indifferent matters that disturbs the church's peace.

Describe mutual submission as a temper rather than a structure — bearing one another's burdens instead of advancing above others or giving laws to one another — with Paul's becoming all things to all men as the example.

debates.question: Is the true reading "the fear of God" or "the fear of Christ"?

sides.position: Christ, on the evidence of the uncials, versions and fathers, though the sense is unchanged
God; the variant was probably introduced by someone who found the received phrase harsh

outliers.note: Alone reports Barrow’s rendering of the phrase as thanksgiving for all persons, and connects it with the Prayer Book’s thanks for God’s kindness to us and to all men.
Alone refuses to exempt kings and governors from mutual subjection, on the ground that their authority exists for the community’s service.

22.pericope_label: Wives, submit yourselves unto your own husbands, as unto the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife, even as Christ is the head of the church: and he is the saviour of the body

schools.summary: Set the verse beside the parallel chain in the earlier letter, where headship is simple lordship, and show that here the headship of Christ over the whole church yields a spiritual unity requiring self-sacrifice in the head as much as obedience to him; mark the qualifying clause as a tremendous difference hastily added.

Refer the qualifying pronoun to Christ and argue that nothing yields a wife more advantage than subjection, so that to refuse the means of her safety is to choose destruction; and narrow the scope of the duty, which is owed to her husband only and to no other.

State the exception first — unless where God forbids — and set out at length what a wife may not obey in, a profligate husband or one using authority to keep her from the means of grace; observe that the inferior party is named first throughout, since inferiors must do their duty whatever their superiors do.
Praise the bond rather than the ordinance, calling the love of husband and wife more despotic than any despotism, since other affections may be strong but this one is strong and unfading.
Sum the whole relation up as unity and love, in which failures on both sides alter nothing of the relation itself.

debates.question: How far does the submission extend?

sides.position: To every lawful thing, but not to what is criminal, nor where a husband would keep his wife from the means of grace
To her husband only, and not to any other man, nor to her children or household

outliers.note: Alone praises the bond itself rather than the ordinance, calling this love more despotic than any despotism because it is not only strong but unfading.
Alone notices that the inferior party is named before the superior throughout the section, and explains it from the general proposition about submission.

25.pericope_label: Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it; that he might sanctify and cleanse it with the washing of water by the word, that he might present it to himself a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing

schools.summary: Make the likeness a condition of authority — only so far as a husband shows the like love, in sympathy, forbearance and abhorrence of tyranny, has he any right to claim lordship — and render the cleansing as in the laver of the water in the Word, while denying that the cleansing takes place in the bath except symbolically.

Guard the sacrament from becoming an idol, since God employs baptism to declare that we are washed and at the same time performs what it represents, but nothing may be ascribed to the sign or the minister that belongs to God; and note that the Pelagians used the presentation to prove perfection in this life, and were answered by Augustine.

Found the husband's authority on his love, which must be such as would lead him to risk his life for her, and extend it to labouring for her salvation; trace the presentation to the royal bride brought in raiment of needlework, with the bridal purifications of Esther behind the cleansing.

Press the timing on candidates for baptism: they are not asked to be without spot before receiving the grace, since it is for remission of sins they were called, but that their conscience, found uncondemned, may concur with the grace when it is given.

debates.question: What is granted to the washing of water?

sides.position: Baptism, in which God declares that we are washed and at the same time performs what it represents — but nothing may be ascribed to sign or minister
Baptism, but the cleansing takes place in it only symbolically
Baptism together with the spoken word — the question of faith and the baptismal formula
Less the inward work of sanctification than justification by the blood and righteousness of Christ

outliers.note: Alone breaks off to defend Paul against the charge that he elsewhere gives a degrading view of marriage, calling this the noblest picture of marriage ever drawn.
Alone applies the “spot or wrinkle” to candidates awaiting baptism, insisting that purity is not required before the grace but that the conscience should be uncondemned when it is given.

28.pericope_label: So ought men to love their wives as their own bodies. For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church: for we are members of his body

schools.summary: Correct the reference of "so" to the love of Christ just described rather than to the comparison following; observe that the figure assumes the Christian estimate of the body as part of the true self, incompatible with the Gnostic view of matter as evil; and pronounce the closing words about flesh and bones no part of the true text.

Put the argument as a syllogism from nature — every man loves himself, no man can love himself without loving his wife, therefore the man who does not love his wife is a monster — and refuse to weaken the closing clause, which is no exaggeration but the simple truth and means more than that Christ shares our nature.

Report the proverbial Jewish maxim that a wife is as her husband's own body; reduce the two verbs to feeding and clothing; and hold the middle ground on the last clause, that Christ partook of our nature as we partook of Adam's.

debates.question: How literally is "of his flesh and of his bones" to be taken?

sides.position: Not literally at all: the union is of attachment, feeling and love, not physical
No exaggeration but the simple truth, meaning more than that Christ shares our nature
The words are not genuine, being wanting in the leading uncials

outliers.note: Alone observes that the comparison presupposes the Christian estimate of the body as part of the true self, and is incompatible with the Gnostic view of matter as the source of evil.

31.pericope_label: For this cause shall a man leave his father and mother, and shall be joined unto his wife, and they two shall be one flesh. This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church

schools.summary: Prefer the simpler reference of "for this cause" to the wife being as the husband's own body, calling the mystical connection too strained even here, and reject as absurd the reading that makes the "man" of the quotation mean Christ; trace the sacramental use of the word mystery to the Latin rendering.

Read the quotation as teaching that members of Christ share his substance, and use it against those who deny such intercourse; then decline to define the mystery at all, being overwhelmed by its depth and unashamed to confess ignorance and admiration together.

Render the joining as gluing or cementing, so that a well-glued board breaks in the solid wood before the joint, and death alone parts husband and wife; and deny that the Latin rendering of mystery makes marriage a sacrament in the sense the Church of Rome uses.

debates.question: Does the Latin rendering of "mystery" make marriage a sacrament?

sides.position: No — the Greek means something concealed and now disclosed, not a sacrament

debates.question: To what does "for this cause" refer?

sides.position: To the wife being as the husband's own body, two verses earlier
To the union of Christ and the church just described
Not, at any rate, so as to make the "man" of the quotation mean Christ

outliers.note: Alone renders the joining as gluing, with the figure of a well-glued board breaking in the solid wood before the joint gives way.

His column carries an editorial note credited to Eadie explaining why the two commands are asymmetrical — each party is enjoined not what is instinctive but what directs the instinct — material that is not Calvin’s own.
